Kavala New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kavala, Greece

Not demolished. Jewish settlement in Kavala began in the 16th century when Ottoman authorities transferred Jews from Budapest; an initially flourishing Ashkenazi community (500+ by the 1540s) was later overtaken by Sephardi refugees from Spain and Portugal, supporting four synagogues by the late 17th century. Population dwindled to a few families by 1740, remaining sparse through the 19th century until mid-century tobacco-trade growth attracted new settlers from Salonika, Monastir, Seres, and Istanbul; the community grew from 24 families (1880) to 230 (over 1,000 people) by 1900. A 1905 school for boys and girls opened with Alliance Israelite Universelle support; population reached 2,350 by 1912, with an active Zionist organization founded that same year after Greek occupation began. Population peaked at 2,500 by 1921, mostly employed in the thriving tobacco industry; by the 1928 census, Kavala was Greece's third-largest Jewish community (2,135), after Salonika and Athens. From 1941-42, hundreds of youths and men were sent to Bulgaria for forced labor; harsh winter conditions in 1942-43 brought epidemics from food, clothing, and medical shortages. On March 3-4, 1943, 1,484 Kavala Jews were deported to Treblinka via Drama and Bulgaria; only 42 survivors remained by 1945. The community was briefly reestablished before final dissolution in 1970, with the last Jewish family leaving in 1979. This cemetery likely dates to the 16th century; in 1934, honorary community president Ist-Dimarnd donated $5,000, allocating $1,000 specifically to cemetery upkeep - double what the community's school received.
